If any other person reaches this milestone before Elon Musk (e.g., Jeff Bezos becomes the first trillionaire), the question will resolve as **No**.

If no individual has a net worth greater than 1 trillion USD before January 1, 2075, or by the time of Musk's death, this question will resolve as **No**

ladder.L1: Forbes maintains a real-time ranking of the world's wealthiest individuals, with the top spots historically rotating among tech founders, retail magnates, and luxury-goods executives. As of the early 2020s, the top five fortunes were concentrated among a handful of men whose wealth derived primarily from large equity stakes in publicly traded or privately held companies.
ladder.L2: As of April 2022, Forbes ranked Elon Musk as the world's wealthiest person at approximately $280 billion, ahead of Jeff Bezos ($180B), Bernard Arnault ($170B), Bill Gates ($130B), and Warren Buffett ($130B). Musk's fortune was tied largely to his stake in Tesla, whose market capitalization had grown rapidly, and to his ownership of SpaceX, a private company whose valuation was rising through successive funding rounds. The gap between Musk and the next-richest individual was roughly $100 billion.
ladder.L3:
By April 2022, Forbes listed Elon Musk as the world's wealthiest individual with a net worth near $280 billion, a lead of approximately $100 billion over Jeff Bezos ($180B) and similarly large margins over Bernard Arnault ($170B), Bill Gates ($130B), and Warren Buffett ($130B). Musk's wealth was concentrated in equity holdings of two high-growth ventures: a roughly 15-20% stake in Tesla, which had appreciated dramatically during 2020-2021 as the company became the most valuable automaker in the world, and a large majority stake in SpaceX, a private company whose valuation was being marked up through successive primary and secondary funding rounds as it expanded Starlink and developed Starship. Musk also held additional interests in The Boring Company and Neuralink.

Analytically, several structural factors distinguished Musk's position from those of other contenders. His wealth was tied to younger, faster-growing companies in sectors (electric vehicles, space launch, satellite internet, AI) with large addressable markets, whereas Bezos's Amazon stake had been partially diluted by divorce and stock sales, Arnault's LVMH grew at the steadier pace of luxury consumer demand, and Gates and Buffett were actively divesting through philanthropy. Musk had also stated publicly that he intended to retain his equity to fund long-term projects such as Mars colonization. The combination of a substantial nominal lead, ownership of multiple appreciating assets, and a stated disinclination to give wealth away were the principal facts a careful observer would have weighed.

title: Will Denis Sassour Nguesso win the 2026 Presidential election in the Republic of the Congo?
background:
Presidential elections in the Republic of the Congo are scheduled for 15 March 2026 (Africa News). Denis Sassou Nguesso, 82, has served as president since 1997 (and previously from 1979 to 1992), making him one of Africa's longest-serving leaders. In late December 2025, the Congolese Labour Party (PCT) formally nominated him as its candidate at its sixth ordinary congress in Brazzaville, framing his candidacy around themes of "stability" and "continuity" (France 24). A 2015 constitutional referendum removed the presidential age limit of 70 and reset term limits, allowing Sassou Nguesso to seek additional five-year terms.

Opposition parties, including the Rally for Democracy and Development (RDD), Movement of Republicans (MR), and People's Party (PAPE), formed the "Alliance for Democratic Alternation in 2026" in April 2023 to contest the election (Africa Press). However, the opposition remains weakened by internal divisions, limited resources, and an uneven political playing field. Two prominent opposition candidates from the 2016 election—Jean-Marie Michel Mokoko and André Okombi Salissa—remain imprisoned. Sassou Nguesso has won every election since 2002, each marred by accusations of fraud and intimidation. International observers from the African Union and European Union have expressed interest in deploying technical assistance teams (The Congo Mail).

Resolution Criteria:

This question will be resolved using official election results announced by the Republic of the Congo's Constitutional Court or reports from credible international news organizations (e.g., Reuters, AFP, France 24). In the event of a contested result, the question will resolve based on official results. The question resolves “Yes” if Denis Sassou Nguesso is declared the winner of the 2026 presidential election, whether in the first round or in a runoff.
resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.randforecastinginitiative.org/questions/1722.

ladder.L1: The Republic of the Congo is scheduled to hold its presidential election on 15 March 2026. Denis Sassou Nguesso, who has been in power since 1997 (and previously from 1979 to 1992), is among the candidates. The country uses a two-round system, and results are certified by the Constitutional Court.
ladder.L2: Denis Sassou Nguesso was formally nominated as the candidate of the ruling Congolese Labour Party (PCT) in December 2025 and has won every presidential election since 2002. A 2015 constitutional referendum removed the age limit and reset term limits, clearing the legal path for his renewed candidacy. The opposition Alliance for Democratic Alternation in 2026 remains fragmented, under-resourced, and weakened by the continued imprisonment of two leading 2016 challengers, Jean-Marie Michel Mokoko and André Okombi Salissa.
ladder.L3:
Denis Sassou Nguesso, 82, has dominated Congolese politics for over four decades, ruling from 1979 to 1992 and continuously since 1997. The 2015 constitutional referendum—criticized by the opposition but ratified by the government—removed both the age cap of 70 and existing term limits, enabling him to contest additional five-year terms. In late December 2025, the ruling Congolese Labour Party (PCT) unanimously endorsed him at its sixth ordinary congress in Brazzaville, with the campaign messaging built around 'stability' and 'continuity.' The PCT controls the parliament, the security apparatus, state media, and most national institutions, including the Constitutional Court that certifies results.

Two of the most credible challengers from the 2016 election, Jean-Marie Michel Mokoko and André Okombi Salissa, remain imprisoned following convictions widely criticized by human rights organizations. Every presidential election Sassou Nguesso has contested since 2002 has been declared a first-round victory for him, typically with margins above 60%, though each has been marred by opposition boycotts, fraud allegations, internet shutdowns, and limited independent international observation. Taken together, the incumbent enters the 15 March 2026 vote with overwhelming structural, institutional, and incumbency advantages relative to a divided opposition operating on an uneven playing field.

title: Will Delcy Rodríguez be President of Venezuela on 30 April 2026?

Venezuela's Supreme Tribunal of Justice ordered Rodríguez to assume presidential duties for 90 days, and the military endorsed her as acting leader (CBS News). Rodríguez had served as Maduro's vice president since 2018 and concurrently held roles as minister of finance and petroleum, positions in which she helped stabilize Venezuela's sanctions-affected economy (NBC News).

Rodríguez's political future remains uncertain. The Trump administration has signaled it will work with her temporarily, though President Trump warned she would "pay a very big price" if she fails to comply with U.S. demands regarding oil access and cooperation (TIME). This question will be resolved as “Yes” if Delcy Rodríguez holds the title of President or Acting President of Venezuela on 30 April 2026, regardless of whether her tenure is recognized as legitimate by foreign governments. title: Will NASA's Artemis II complete its mission successfully before 2027?
resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as **Yes** if Artemis II achieves a closest-approach altitude ≤20,000 km above the lunar surface during the mission and returns to Earth with no loss of crew before January 1, 2027.

ladder.L1: Artemis II is NASA's planned crewed mission to fly four astronauts around the Moon, building on the uncrewed Artemis I test flight that completed a lunar flyby in late 2022. The mission uses NASA's Orion spacecraft and the Space Launch System (SLS) heavy-lift rocket, and is intended as a precursor to a crewed lunar landing on Artemis III.
ladder.L2: As of late 2025, NASA had accelerated the Artemis II launch target from April 2026 to February 2026, with the official mission page listing a 'No Later Than April 2026' date. The mission profile is a roughly 10-day lunar flyby taking the crew about 7,500 km beyond the far side of the Moon — well inside the 20,000 km closest-approach threshold specified in the resolution criteria. The SLS rocket and Orion capsule had been stacked and integrated, and the uncrewed Artemis I had previously demonstrated the same basic trajectory and return successfully.
ladder.L3: By late 2025, Artemis II hardware was in advanced stages of preparation: the SLS core stage, boosters, and Orion crew capsule had been integrated at Kennedy Space Center, the four-person crew (Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen) had been training for over two years, and NASA had taken the unusual step in March 2025 of pulling the launch date forward by two months — from April 2026 to February 2026 — signaling internal confidence in schedule margin. The official NASA mission page as of December 5, 2025 listed the launch as 'No Later Than April 2026,' giving roughly 8–10 months of schedule buffer before the January 1, 2027 resolution deadline. The planned trajectory is a free-return lunar flyby passing approximately 7,500 km beyond the far side of the Moon, which corresponds to a closest-approach altitude far below the 20,000 km threshold in the resolution criteria. The uncrewed Artemis I mission in 2022 had already validated the SLS launch, Orion's trans-lunar injection, lunar flyby, and reentry/splashdown sequence; post-flight analysis identified heat-shield charring and some component issues, all of which NASA addressed in subsequent reviews before clearing Artemis II. Taken together, the hardware readiness, accelerated schedule, substantial buffer to the deadline, and the mission profile's natural compatibility with the altitude criterion form a coherent factual picture for the forecaster to weigh.

title: Will the WHO declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in 2026?
background:
According to [the WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/emergencies-international-health-regulations-and-emergency-committees): 

> A PHEIC is defined in the IHR (2005) as, “an extraordinary event which is determined to constitute a public health risk to other States through the international spread of disease and to potentially require a coordinated international response”. This definition implies a situation that is:

> * serious, sudden, unusual or unexpected;
> * carries implications for public health beyond the affected State’s national border; and
> * may require immediate international action.

In articles adopted in 2024, WHO further [added](https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/pandemic-prevention--preparedness-and-response-accord) a "pandemic emergency" to its PHEIC mechanisms:

> [The amendments to the International Health Regulations](https://apps.who.int/gb/ebwha/pdf_files/WHA77/A77_ACONF14-en.pdf), agreed by the Seventy-seventh World Health Assembly on 1 June 2024, include the definition of a Pandemic Emergency, which represents the new highest level of alarm contained within the IHR and available for use by the WHO Director-General.

> The Pandemic Emergency definition builds on the existing mechanisms of the IHR, including the determination of public health emergency of international concern.

> A Pandemic Emergency aims to trigger a more effective international collaboration in response to events that are at risk of becoming, or have become, a pandemic.

In January 2025, the Metaculus Community [was](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/30763/will-an-h5-pheic-be-declared-by-the-who-before-2026/) as high as a 30% assessed probability that WHO could declare a PHEIC before year-end over H5 avian influenza, though it declined to less than 10% by April. In November 2025, the first human known to be infected with the H5N5 strain [died](https://abcnews.go.com/US/1st-human-infected-h5n5-strain-bird-flu-dies/story?id=127774354) in Washington state.

Historically, PHEICs were declared in 7 out of the 17 years in the 2009-2025 period (41%):

| Number | Outbreak                                                                                                                                      | Pathogen                       | PHEIC declaration date | PHEIC ended / ongoing |
| ------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ---------------------- | --------------------- |
| 1      | [2009–2010 H1N1 (swine flu) pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_swine_flu_pandemic)                                                  | Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09         | 26 Apr 2009            | 10 Aug 2010           |
| 2      | [Polio (2014–present) PHEIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_health_emergency_of_international_concern#Polio_%282014%E2%80%93present%29) | Wild poliovirus & cVDPV        | 5 May 2014             | Ongoing               |
| 3      | [Western African Ebola epidemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_African_Ebola_epidemic)                                                | Ebola virus (Zaire ebolavirus) | 8 Aug 2014             | 29 Mar 2016           |
| 4      | [2015–16 Zika virus epidemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015%E2%80%9316_Zika_virus_epidemic)                                              | Zika virus                     | 1 Feb 2016             | 18 Nov 2016           |
| 5      | [Kivu Ebola epidemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kivu_Ebola_epidemic)                                                                      | Ebola virus (Zaire ebolavirus) | 17 Jul 2019            | 26 Jun 2020           |
| 6      | [COVID‑19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic)                                                                          | SARS‑CoV‑2                     | 30 Jan 2020
resolution_criteria: This question resolves as **Yes** if before January 1, 2027, the World Health Organization (WHO) declares a new Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC).

ladder.L1: The WHO Director-General can declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) under the International Health Regulations (2005) when an extraordinary event poses a public health risk through international disease spread and may require coordinated international response. Between 2009 and 2025, PHEICs were declared in 7 of 17 years, an annual base rate of roughly 41%. In 2024, WHO adopted amendments to the IHR that added a 'pandemic emergency' as a higher tier built on the existing PHEIC mechanism.
ladder.L2: As of late 2025, multiple disease threats were under active WHO monitoring, including ongoing concerns about H5 avian influenza (with the first human H5N5 infection reported fatal in Washington state in November 2025) and continued mpox transmission in parts of Africa. The historical base rate of PHEIC declarations is approximately 41% per year over 2009–2025, and WHO's 2024 IHR amendments expanded the alert architecture around PHEICs. WHO Emergency Committees met repeatedly during 2025 on several pathogens of concern.
ladder.L3: Several factors shaped the landscape going into and through 2026. First, the historical base rate is substantial: PHEICs were declared in 7 of the 17 years between 2009 and 2025 (~41%), and multiple PHEICs (including mpox, declared again in August 2024) remained active or recently active heading into the question window. Second, the threat environment featured several pathogens already under WHO scrutiny: H5N1 avian influenza had spread widely in dairy cattle and wild mammals with sporadic human cases in North America, and in November 2025 the first known human H5N5 case died in Washington state; mpox clade I continued to circulate in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and neighboring countries; and Marburg, Ebola, and cholera outbreaks were intermittently reported across Africa. Third, the institutional context had shifted: the 2024 IHR amendments formalized a 'pandemic emergency' tier built on the PHEIC mechanism, and WHO Emergency Committees were convening regularly. Taken together, the combination of a high historical base rate, multiple simultaneously active zoonotic and outbreak threats, and an expanded alert framework meant the conditions under which the Director-General has historically determined a PHEIC were present in more than one pathogen track during the year.

title: Will an AI model reach a 3 hour time horizon with 80% reliability during 2026?
background:
[METR](https://metr.org/) is an AI model evaluation and threat research organisation that studies AI capabilities and their ability to conduct AI research and self-improve.

METR regularly tests released models for their threat capacity, which includes measuring their ability to complete realistic software and research tasks reliably. For each task, they measure how long it takes humans with relevant expertise to complete it, then see which tasks different models can solve. By fitting a curve of model success against human task duration, they define each model's "[time horizons](https://metr.org/blog/2025-03-19-measuring-ai-ability-to-complete-long-tasks/)": the longest task length (in human time) on which the model can succeed with around 50% or 80% probability.

Their results show that these horizons have been growing exponentially over time. As of December 2025 the highest time horizon with an 80% chance of success is 31 minutes by [GPT-5.1-Codex-Max](https://evaluations.metr.org/gpt-5-1-codex-max-report/), a 5x improvement from 2024's best performer GPT-o1.
resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as **Yes** if, during 2026, [METR estimates](https://metr.org/blog/2025-03-19-measuring-ai-ability-to-complete-long-tasks/) that an AI model has a time horizon of ≥3 hours at 80% reliability, i.e. the AI has an estimated ≥80% reliability on tasks requiring human experts ≥3 hours to solve.

ladder.L1: METR is an AI evaluation organization that measures models' 'time horizons'—the length of human task that a model can complete with a given reliability. They periodically publish updated horizon measurements for newly released frontier models and have documented a trend of growing horizons over the past several years.
ladder.L2: METR's data shows AI time horizons (at both 50% and 80% reliability) have been growing roughly exponentially, with the 80% horizon increasing about 5x from 2024 to late 2025. As of December 2025, GPT-5.1-Codex-Max holds the top 80% horizon at 31 minutes, and frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind) have been releasing successor models on a cadence of every few months, each typically improving on METR's benchmarks.
ladder.L3:
METR's longitudinal measurements show that the 80% time horizon for frontier AI models has been doubling on a timescale of roughly 4-6 months, with GPT-5.1-Codex-Max reaching 31 minutes in late 2025—about 5x the 2024 leader GPT-o1. The 50% horizon has consistently run several times longer than the 80% horizon. Frontier labs released multiple capability jumps in 2025 (the GPT-5 family, Claude successors, Gemini updates), and METR has been promptly evaluating each release, meaning new horizon data points arrive frequently.

Factually, reaching a 3-hour 80% horizon from a 31-minute starting point requires roughly a 5.8x increase. Given the observed doubling pattern over recent METR measurements and the continued pace of frontier model releases scheduled through 2026, the gap between the late-2025 state of the art and a 3-hour threshold is within the range of growth that the historical METR trend has exhibited over comparable time spans.

title: Will any political party or coalition acquire a supermajority in the 2026 Hungarian parliamentary elections?
background:
In 2010, Viktor Orbán’s party, Fidesz–Hungarian Civic Alliance, together with [its ally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidesz%E2%80%93KDNP) the Christian Democratic People’s Party (KDNP), [won 52.7% of the vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Hungarian_parliamentary_election) but—because of the electoral system—secured 263 of 386 seats, a ⅔ supermajority, giving the party the ability to amend the constitution without the support of other parties.

And indeed the government then amended the constitution, enacting [the Fundamental Law of 2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Hungary#2011_Constitution), under which: (i) Parliament shrank from 386 to 199 seats; (ii) Single-round voting replaced the old two-round system; (iii) a “Winner compensation” system was introduced; and (iv) Redistricting occurred. With these changes, a party with \~45–50% of the popular vote can acquire a two-thirds constitutional supermajority. Under the old rules, such a feat was much less likely.

Hungary's [electoral system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_system_of_Hungary#National_Assembly_elections) is neither purely majoritarian (e.g., winner-take-all, district-based elections), nor purely proportional (e.g., a party-list election where districts don't matter). Instead, it is a mixed system that favours the majoritarian approach. Of the 199 seats, 106 are District Seats (elected via first-past-the-post voting) and 93 are List Seats (elected based on total national proportion). But Hungary's system [differs from other Mixed Systems such as Germany's](https://archive.nytimes.com/krugman.blogs.nytimes.com/2014/02/28/hungary-an-election-in-question-part-3/) due to the "winner compensation" system under which the surplus votes for the winner in a district are added into the national votes, allowing the party that won the district to win extra List Seats as well. With the current electoral system in Germany the list tier is used to *correct* toward proportionality. In Hungary, the surplus mechanism can *magnify* the dominance of the district winner.

The [next Hungarian parliamentary elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Hungarian_parliamentary_election) are scheduled for April 12, 2026.
resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as Yes if any party or coalition acquires a ⅔ supermajority (i.e., at least 133 seats) in the first Hungarian parliamentary elections held after this question opens, according to official election results.

ladder.L1: Hungary's next parliamentary elections are scheduled for April 12, 2026, using a mixed electoral system in which 106 of 199 seats are allocated via first-past-the-post district contests and 93 via national party lists. Since 2010, Fidesz–KDNP, led by Viktor Orbán, has governed Hungary and has won every subsequent parliamentary election.
ladder.L2: Hungary's electoral system includes a 'winner compensation' mechanism that channels surplus district votes back into the list tier, amplifying rather than correcting the dominance of the leading party; under these rules, a party winning roughly 45–50% of the vote can secure a two-thirds supermajority of the 199 seats. Fidesz–KDNP obtained such a supermajority in 2010, 2014, 2018, and 2022. The party retains control of substantial state and media resources and an extensive district-level political machine going into the April 12, 2026 election.
ladder.L3:
Hungary's 2011 Fundamental Law restructured the electoral system in ways that systematically magnify the seat share of the leading party: parliament was reduced from 386 to 199 seats, two-round voting was replaced with single-round first-past-the-post in the 106 district seats, districts were redrawn, and a 'winner compensation' rule was introduced under which surplus votes for district winners are added to their national list totals. Analysts have noted that, unlike Germany's mixed system which uses the list tier to correct toward proportionality, Hungary's list tier can further reward the district-winning party, such that roughly 45–50% of the vote can translate into the 133 seats needed for a two-thirds supermajority.

Fidesz–KDNP, in power since 2010, achieved a two-thirds supermajority in the 2010, 2014, 2018, and 2022 elections, the latter three under the post-2011 rules. The Hungarian opposition has historically struggled to coordinate across ideological lines, and the district map plus winner-compensation tend to penalize fragmented opposition fields. Fidesz also enters the 2026 cycle with substantial incumbency advantages, including control over much of the media landscape, state administrative resources, and an established nationwide district organization.

Supply chain risk is defined in the statute to mean the risk that an adversary may sabotage or subvert the relevant national security system.

Separately, under [41 U.S.C § 4713](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/41/4713), the head of an executive agency may exclude a "source" from competing for government contacts for certain information technology or telecommunications systems, in order to reduce supply chain risk. Similarly here, supply chain risk is defined to mean the risk that a person may sabotage or manipulate the system(s) in question. By law, a party excluded under this statute [may petition for judicial review](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/41/1327). In September 2025, [Acronis AG, a Swedish cybersecurity and data protection company](https://natlawreview.com/article/order-first-fascsa-order-has-been-issued-odni), became the first entity known to be excluded under this law.

ladder.L1: Anthropic is an American AI company founded in 2021 that has increasingly engaged with U.S. national security customers, including allowing intelligence and defense use of its Claude model. U.S. law provides two mechanisms (10 U.S.C. § 3252 and 41 U.S.C. § 4713) for excluding sources from government contracts to address supply chain risk.
ladder.L2: In September 2025, the first known exclusion order under 41 U.S.C. § 4713 was issued against Acronis AG, demonstrating that the federal government had begun actively using the supply chain risk exclusion authority. ladder.L3:
Two converging factual threads are relevant. First, the federal government's supply chain risk exclusion authorities have moved from dormant to active: 41 U.S.C. § 4713 was used for the first known time in September 2025 against Acronis AG, a Swedish cybersecurity firm, indicating that ODNI and executive agencies were now willing to issue FASCSA exclusion orders against commercial technology vendors. title: In Louisiana v. Callais, will SCOTUS strike down Louisiana’s two majority-Black districts, restoring a GOP-leaning map?
resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as **Yes** if, before October 5, 2026, in [Louisiana, Appellant v Phillip Callais, et al.](https://www.supremecourt.gov/docket/docketfiles/html/public/24-109.html), the United States Supreme Court holds that the Louisiana congressional [map](https://redist.legis.la.gov/2024_Files/Act2Congress/District%20and%20Split%20Parish%20Maps/Act%202%20\(SB8\)%201st%20ES%202024%20-%20Congressional%20Districts%20-%20Statewide.pdf) for 2024 ([SB8](https://redist.legis.la.gov/2024_Files/2024CONGRESSACT2)) is illegal, unconstitutional, or otherwise invalid under the US Constitution or federal law. 

If, before October 5, 2026, the Court issues a final disposition of Louisiana v. Callais affirming the SB8 map, or dismissing, vacating or remanding the case on other grounds, then the question resolves as **No**.

ladder.L1: Louisiana v. Callais is a Supreme Court case challenging Louisiana's 2024 congressional map (SB8), which created two majority-Black districts out of six. The case involves the intersection of the Voting Rights Act's Section 2 requirements and the Equal Protection Clause's restrictions on racial gerrymandering. The Supreme Court heard arguments in the case during its 2024-2025 term.
ladder.L2: After initial oral argument in March 2025, the Supreme Court took the unusual step of ordering reargument for the October 2025 Term and directed the parties to brief additional questions, including whether Louisiana's intentional creation of a second majority-Black district violates the Fourteenth or Fifteenth Amendments. The Court's conservative majority has in recent years narrowed race-conscious remedies in other contexts (e.g., Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard), and Justice Thomas has repeatedly written separately questioning the constitutionality of Section 2 vote-dilution remedies. Several justices, including Kavanaugh in his Allen v. Milligan concurrence, signaled that race-based districting may not be permissible indefinitely.
ladder.L3:
Louisiana v. Callais arrived at the Supreme Court after a three-judge district court panel struck down SB8's two majority-Black-district map as an unconstitutional racial gerrymander, while earlier litigation (Robinson v. Ardoin) had forced Louisiana to draw a second majority-Black district to comply with Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. The state thus found itself caught between competing federal mandates. After oral argument in March 2025, the Court did not decide the case in the 2024-2025 Term; instead, in the summer of 2025, it restored the case to the calendar for reargument and ordered supplemental briefing on broader constitutional questions, including whether the State's intentional creation of a second majority-Black congressional district violates the Fourteenth or Fifteenth Amendment.

The Court's recent trajectory on race-conscious policy is relevant context: in Students for Fair Admissions (2023), the Court ended race-conscious college admissions; in Shelby County (2013), it gutted Section 5 preclearance; and although Allen v. Milligan (2023) preserved Section 2 in the Alabama context by a 5-4 vote, Justice Kavanaugh's concurrence explicitly flagged that race-based remedies may have temporal limits, and Justice Thomas has long argued Section 2 does not authorize vote-dilution claims at all. The decision to order reargument with expanded constitutional questions, rather than resolve the case on narrower Gingles-application grounds, signaled the Court's interest in addressing the larger tension between Section 2 and the Equal Protection Clause as applied to Louisiana's map.

title: Will the FDA have authorized a medical device that incorporates LLM-based functionality by 31 March 2026?
background:
The FDA has yet to approve any medical devices incorporating Large Language Model (LLM) functionality as clinical decision support systems (Nature Digital Medicine). While the FDA has authorized over 950 AI/ML-enabled medical devices, many for radiology applications, none use generative AI or LLMs (MDR Regulator, HIMSS). However, the FDA has indicated it will explore methods to identify and tag devices incorporating LLM functionality in future updates to its AI device database (FDA).

The regulatory challenges for LLM-based devices are significant. Traditional FDA authorization requires devices to have specific indications for use, but LLMs can respond to broad queries, potentially providing "off label" responses relative to an approved indication (Nature Digital Medicine). Additionally, current regulatory frameworks don't allow continuous updating of software and AI-based medical devices, though the FDA, Health Canada, and UK MHRA are working on Predetermined Change Control Plans (PCCPs) to address this (FDA, Hardian Health). At least one company has sought FDA feedback on an LLM-based device – Contrast Llama, for detecting contrast agents in CT scans (Innolitics). 

Resolution Criteria:  
This question will be resolved using FDA announcements, approval documentation (e.g., in the Devices@FDA database), and/or official government or regulatory body press releases regarding the authorization of devices with LLM-based functionality. The device must receive standard FDA clearance or approval without limitation to temporary, investigational, or humanitarian uses.
resolution_criteria:
What counts as "LLM-based functionality":

  1. Any level of LLM integration at approval: Any incorporation of an LLM in the device at the time of FDA authorization would count, even if used for minor features like natural language interfaces, report summarization, or user interaction. However, adding LLM functionality after initial approval (e.g., through an app update) would not count.
  2. Multimodal models included: Foundation models that are multimodal count as "LLM-based functionality" as long as they are used in their text or language generation capacity.
  3. No minimum model size: Smaller, fine-tuned, or constrained language models count. There is no lower bound on the number of parameters the model must have. Models do not need to exhibit broad generative or conversational capabilities to qualify.

The resolution criteria has also been updated to say that the device must receive standard FDA clearance or approval without limitation to temporary, investigational, or humanitarian uses. (The term "specific medical purposes" has been removed from this line.)

ladder.L1: The FDA maintains a public list of AI/ML-enabled medical devices that have received authorization. Large language models (LLMs) are a relatively recent class of AI systems that have attracted growing interest for healthcare applications, raising new regulatory questions about how they fit into existing device authorization pathways.
ladder.L2: As of the question's launch, the FDA had authorized over 950 AI/ML-enabled medical devices, but according to public reporting and FDA's own communications, none of these incorporated generative AI or LLM functionality. The FDA has signaled it is still developing approaches to evaluate LLM-based devices, including challenges around indications-for-use specificity and continuous model updating, and frameworks like Predetermined Change Control Plans (PCCPs) are still being formalized.
ladder.L3:
Several converging facts shape the evidentiary picture. First, the FDA's published list of AI/ML-enabled medical devices (numbering over 950 by early 2025) contained no devices using generative AI or LLMs, and the agency itself stated it was still working on methods to identify and tag such devices in future database updates. Second, peer-reviewed analyses (e.g., in Nature Digital Medicine) and regulatory commentary highlighted structural obstacles: traditional FDA clearance requires narrowly defined indications for use, while LLMs are inherently general-purpose and can produce 'off-label' outputs, complicating substantial-equivalence and safety determinations. Third, supporting frameworks like PCCPs—which would allow controlled post-market model updates—were still in draft or early-implementation stages at the FDA, Health Canada, and the UK MHRA.

Industry activity suggested early-stage rather than imminent authorizations: at least one company (Contrast Llama) had sought FDA pre-submission feedback for an LLM-based device, but pre-submission engagement typically precedes formal 510(k), De Novo, or PMA submissions by many months, and clearance timelines for novel AI devices have historically run a year or more from submission. Taken together, the absence of any prior LLM-incorporating authorization, unresolved regulatory frameworks, and the early stage of known industry pipelines define the landscape leading up to the 31 March 2026 deadline.

title: Will any branch of the U.S. military have hypersonic weapons operationally deployed with field units, aboard naval vessels, or on aircraft by 30 April 2026?
background:
Hypersonic weapons, which travel at speeds exceeding Mach 5 (approximately 3,800 miles per hour), represent a new class of weaponry for the U.S. military designed to strike time-critical, heavily defended targets with minimal warning. The U.S. is developing three primary hypersonic weapons programs: the Army's Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon (LRHW), also known as Dark Eagle; the Navy's Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS); and the Air Force's Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM) (Army Recognition).

As of December 2025, the Army's Dark Eagle program is closest to operational deployment. The 5th Battalion, 3rd Field Artillery Regiment at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Washington, received ground equipment in 2021 and has been training on the system while awaiting live missiles (Defense News). According to the Army's program executive officer for missiles and space, the final batch of missiles for the first battery was expected to be delivered by the end of December 2025 (Interesting Engineering). The Army and Navy conducted a successful end-to-end flight test of the Common Hypersonic Glide Body in December 2024 at Cape Canaveral (Wikipedia). However, as of March 2025, decisions on when the system will achieve Initial Operational Capability (IOC) remain pending approval from senior Army leadership following the presidential transition (Breaking Defense).

The Navy's CPS program has experienced delays, with testing aboard USS Zumwalt now projected for 2027 or 2028 rather than the original 2025 timeline (USNI News). The Air Force's hypersonic programs remain in development and testing phases, with fiscal year 2026 funding designated for continued development rather than operational deployment (DefenseScoop).

Resolution Criteria:
This question will be resolved using official announcements from the U.S. Department of Defense, military service branch press releases and official websites, and credible reporting from established defense media outlets including Defense News, Breaking Defense, USNI News, and Military.com.

This question will resolve “Yes” if, on or before 30 April 2026, reports indicate that any branch of the U.S. military has hypersonic weapons operationally deployed with field units or aboard naval vessels.

Operational deployment will be confirmed by official U.S. military announcements declaring Initial Operational Capability (IOC) or equivalent operational status for a hypersonic weapon system. If official announcements are unavailable, administrators will rely on credible defense media reporting, citing military officials or sources, confirming that a hypersonic weapon system has achieved operational s
resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.randforecastinginitiative.org/questions/1703.

ladder.L1: The U.S. military is pursuing several hypersonic weapons programs across the Army, Navy, and Air Force, including the Army's Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon (Dark Eagle), the Navy's Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS), and the Air Force's Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM). These programs are at varying stages of development, with the Army's Dark Eagle generally considered the furthest along toward fielding. Hypersonic weapons are defined as systems that travel at speeds exceeding Mach 5.
ladder.L2: The Army's Dark Eagle battery at Joint Base Lewis-McChord received its ground equipment in 2021 but has spent years training without live missiles, with the final batch of missiles for the first battery expected by the end of December 2025. As of March 2025, decisions on when Dark Eagle will achieve Initial Operational Capability remained pending senior Army leadership approval following the presidential transition. The Navy's Conventional Prompt Strike program has slipped, with testing aboard USS Zumwalt now projected for 2027 or 2028 rather than 2025, and the Air Force's HACM remains in development and testing phases.
ladder.L3:
Among the three principal U.S. hypersonic programs, only the Army's Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon (Dark Eagle) has been credibly close to fielding in the near term. The first unit, the 5th Battalion, 3rd Field Artillery Regiment at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, received ground equipment (launchers, transport vehicles, command-and-control) back in 2021 and has been training without live rounds for years. The Army and Navy conducted a successful end-to-end flight test of the Common Hypersonic Glide Body in December 2024, and Army officials stated the final missile deliveries to complete the first battery were anticipated by the end of December 2025. However, as of March 2025, the formal fielding plan and Initial Operational Capability decision for Dark Eagle were still awaiting approval from senior Army leadership after the presidential transition, and prior IOC targets had already slipped multiple times.

The other services are further behind. The Navy's Conventional Prompt Strike program, which would put hypersonic weapons aboard USS Zumwalt and later Virginia-class submarines, saw its at-sea testing timeline pushed from 2025 to 2027 or 2028. The Air Force's HACM and related efforts remain in development and flight-testing, without a unit equipped for operational employment. Taken together, the publicly available record shows persistent schedule slips, a pending IOC decision for the most mature program, and no service having yet declared a hypersonic weapon operationally deployed with a field unit, ship, or aircraft.

title: Will  an attempt be made to fire Jerome Powell before the end of his term?
resolution_criteria: This question resolves as **Yes** if President Donald Trump or the US government publicly states before May 1, 2026 that Jerome Powell is terminated, dismissed, or forcibly replaced (resignations or voluntary departures do not count) before his scheduled term end date of May 15, 2026, from either his role as Chair of the [Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System](https://www.federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed.htm) (FRB) or his role as Chair of the [Federal Open Market Committee](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomc.htm) (FOMC).

ladder.L1: Jerome Powell serves as Chair of the Federal Reserve Board and of the FOMC, with both terms scheduled to end on May 15, 2026. He was first appointed by President Trump in 2017 and renominated by President Biden in 2021, being confirmed by wide bipartisan margins both times.
ladder.L2: After Powell signaled in April 2025 that the Fed would remain patient on rate cuts in light of Trump's sweeping new tariffs, Trump publicly attacked him, writing that 'Powell's termination cannot come fast enough' and calling him a 'major loser.' However, the Federal Reserve Act provides for removal of a Governor only 'for cause,' and the Supreme Court's May 2025 order in Trump v. Wilcox specifically signaled that the Fed is a 'uniquely structured, quasi-private entity' whose leadership enjoys special protection from at-will removal. Powell himself stated publicly that he would not resign if asked and that he believed his removal was 'not permitted under the law.'
ladder.L3:
Tensions between President Trump and Chair Powell escalated sharply in April 2025 after Powell, citing the inflationary risks of Trump's 'Liberation Day' tariffs, said the Fed would hold off on cutting rates. Trump responded on Truth Social with posts calling Powell 'Too Late' and 'a major loser,' and saying 'Powell's termination cannot come fast enough.' Over the following months, Trump and allies floated additional pressure tactics — including criticism of the Fed's headquarters renovation costs and an attempted removal of Fed Governor Lisa Cook — but stopped short of issuing an order purporting to fire Powell himself. Senior administration officials, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and NEC Director Kevin Hassett, publicly indicated the administration was instead focused on the search for Powell's successor when his term ends in May 2026.

Legally, the Federal Reserve Act allows removal of a Board member only 'for cause,' and in May 2025 the Supreme Court, in staying lower-court rulings concerning removals at other independent agencies, went out of its way to describe the Federal Reserve as a 'uniquely structured, quasi-private entity' deserving of distinct treatment — language widely read as shielding Powell. Powell stated publicly that he would not resign and that he did not believe the president had legal authority to fire him, and market reactions to Trump's April posts (a sharp sell-off in the dollar and Treasuries) were reported to have given the White House pause. Taken together, the public record shows intense rhetorical pressure but no formal action by the president or U.S. government purporting to terminate Powell.

title: Will the average Arctic sea ice extent for March 2026 be the lowest on record for that month according to the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)?
background:
Arctic sea ice extent in March—when the annual maximum typically occurs—has declined sharply in recent decades as the Arctic warms faster than the rest of the planet (NSIDC). The National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) maintains the Sea Ice Index, a satellite-based record of Arctic sea ice extent dating back to November 1978.

March 2025 set a new record low for the month, with an average extent of 14.1 million square kilometers, breaking the previous record of 14.28 million square kilometers set in 2017 (NSIDC). The 2025 annual maximum of 14.33 million square kilometers on 22 March 2025 was the lowest in the 47-year satellite record, falling 1.31 million square kilometers below the 1981-2010 average and 80,000 square kilometers below the previous record set in 2017 (NSIDC). The long-term trend shows March sea ice extent declining at 2.5% per decade relative to the 1981-2010 average, with nearly all March monthly averages since 2004 falling well below the historical average (NSIDC).

Resolution Criteria:

This question will resolve using monthly data from the National Snow and Ice Data Center's Sea Ice Index.

This question will resolve "Yes" if the monthly average Arctic sea ice extent for March 2026, as reported by NSIDC in the Sea Ice Index, is lower than the March 2025 record.

For the purposes of this question, "monthly average extent" refers to the official monthly mean extent value published by NSIDC in the Sea Ice Index data files, typically released in early April following the end of March. If NSIDC revises its methodology or dataset in a way that materially changes historical extent values, resolution will be based on the revised dataset's comparison of March 2026 to the lowest March on record in that revised dataset.
resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.randforecastinginitiative.org/questions/1723.

ladder.L1: Arctic sea ice extent reaches its annual maximum in March and has been measured by satellites since 1978, with NSIDC publishing monthly averages in its Sea Ice Index. March extent has shown a long-term declining trend of roughly 2.5% per decade relative to the 1981-2010 average.
ladder.L2: March 2025 set a new record low monthly average Arctic sea ice extent of 14.1 million square kilometers, breaking the 2017 record of 14.28 million sq km by about 180,000 sq km—a relatively large margin compared to typical year-to-year fluctuations. Despite the long-term decline of about 2.5% per decade, new March monthly records have historically been set only intermittently (e.g., 2015, 2017, 2025), with most years falling above the most recent record even when below the long-term average.
ladder.L3:
According to NSIDC, March 2025 set a new record low Arctic sea ice monthly average extent at 14.1 million square kilometers, surpassing the previous March record (14.28 million sq km, set in 2017) by roughly 180,000 sq km. The 2025 annual maximum of 14.33 million sq km on 22 March 2025 was 1.31 million sq km below the 1981-2010 average and only 80,000 sq km below the 2017 maximum. The long-term March trend is a decline of about 2.5% per decade relative to the 1981-2010 average, and nearly all March averages since 2004 have been well below that historical baseline.

Historically, although the underlying trend is downward, new March monthly record lows have been set only sporadically in the satellite record (notably 2015, 2017, and 2025), with many intervening years coming in above the most recent record despite the overall decline. Year-to-year variability in March extent is driven substantially by winter weather patterns, regional wind fields, and sea surface temperatures in the Barents, Bering, and Okhotsk Seas, which can produce swings larger than the average annual trend. Consequently, even after a record-low March, subsequent Marches have frequently rebounded somewhat relative to the new record.

> The purported offenses ran the gamut. One Democrat plotted to handpick his successor, while another texted with the convicted sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein. A Republican was accused by his colleagues of contracting abuses, faking his military honors and assaulting a woman at his apartment. A third Democrat was indicted on charges that she stole Federal Emergency Management Agency funds.

> It was a vivid illustration of how official House rebukes, once exceedingly rare and mostly a matter of consensus for the most egregious conduct or illegal acts by a sitting member of Congress, have become commonplace in recent years.

> Members of both parties have stepped up the use of censure resolutions as a partisan political weapon. Many of them include accusations by lawmakers that in the past would first have been investigated by the House Ethics Committee — and often weighed in court — before reaching the floor if found to be valid.

For base rate information, please see [List of Individuals Expelled, Censured, or Reprimanded in the U.S. House of Representatives](https://history.house.gov/Institution/Discipline/Expulsion-Censure-Reprimand/)
resolution_criteria: This question resolves as **Yes** if, before April 1, 2026, the United States House of Representatives passes a resolution censuring, expelling or reprimanding a sitting Representative. If no such resolution passes before that date, the question resolves as **No**.

ladder.L1: The US House of Representatives has the constitutional authority to discipline its members through expulsion, censure, or reprimand, with such resolutions typically requiring a simple majority vote (two-thirds for expulsion). Historically these formal rebukes were rare, but their use has increased notably over the past several Congresses. The current Congress has seen heightened partisan tensions and several high-profile controversies involving sitting members.
ladder.L2: By late November 2025, multiple House members had introduced privileged resolutions to censure or otherwise punish colleagues, including Rep. Nancy Mace's censure resolution against Rep. Cory Mills and resolutions targeting Democratic members over alleged misconduct. News coverage from the Wall Street Journal and New York Times described a chaotic atmosphere in which censure votes have proliferated and become a routine partisan tool. The House has used procedural moves—such as motions to table or refer to the Ethics Committee—to dispose of many such resolutions without an up-or-down vote on the underlying punishment.
ladder.L3:
Censure and reprimand resolutions in the House had grown increasingly common in the 118th and 119th Congresses, with members of both parties using the privileged-resolution mechanism to force floor consideration of rebukes against colleagues. In November 2025, the Wall Street Journal and New York Times reported a flurry of such efforts: Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) pushed a censure resolution against Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.) over alleged contracting abuses, falsified military honors, and an alleged assault; Democrats faced resolutions over matters including communications with Jeffrey Epstein, a plan to handpick a successor, and an indictment involving alleged theft of FEMA funds. Leadership in both parties was reported to be frustrated by the proliferation of these votes and largely unable to prevent them from reaching the floor.

Historically, even when censure resolutions are introduced as privileged, the House frequently disposes of them through motions to table or by referring them to the Committee on Ethics, which prevents a direct vote on the censure itself. The November 2025 reporting emphasized the chaotic procedural environment but did not document a completed censure, expulsion, or reprimand vote passing during that period; many of the resolutions described were either pending, referred, or tabled. The base rate for a successful House discipline action in any given multi-month window has risen in recent Congresses, but successful passage still depends on majority support, which is uncertain when resolutions target members of the majority party or are seen as partisan overreach.

title: Will Arizona Senator Mark Kelly, who urged troops to defy "illegal" orders, be recalled to active duty in the US military before April 1, 2026?
background:

Mark Kelly of Arizona over possible breaches of military law after the former Navy pilot joined a handful of other lawmakers [in a video](https://apnews.com/article/trump-military-traitors-sedition-illegal-orders-c5fc3c5bd2fbc6b1204550e4203c24b2) that called for troops to defy “illegal orders.”

> The Pentagon’s statement, posted on social media, cited a federal law that allows retired service members to be recalled to active duty on orders of the defense secretary for possible court martial or other measures.

> It is extraordinary for the Pentagon, which until President Donald Trump’s second term had usually gone out of its way to act and appear apolitical, to directly threaten a sitting member of Congress with investigation. It comes after Trump ramped up the rhetoric by accusing the lawmakers of sedition “punishable by DEATH” in a social media post days after the video was released last week.
resolution_criteria: This question resolves as **Yes** if, before April 1, 2026, according to [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions) Senator Mark Kelly has been placed on Active Duty status in the [United States Armed Forces](https://www.war.gov/About/Our-Forces/).

ladder.L1: Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona is a former Navy combat pilot and retired Captain who served in the Gulf War and later became a NASA astronaut before entering politics. In November 2025, he and several other Democratic lawmakers with military or intelligence backgrounds released a video urging US service members to refuse 'illegal orders.' The video prompted sharp rebukes from President Trump and senior Pentagon officials.
ladder.L2: After the video's release, the Pentagon announced on November 24, 2025 that it was investigating Kelly and cited a federal statute permitting the Secretary of Defense to recall retired service members to active duty for court-martial or other disciplinary proceedings. Recalling a sitting US senator to active duty would be historically unprecedented and would face significant legal hurdles, including questions about the Speech or Debate Clause and the separation of powers. As of late November 2025, the Pentagon's statement described an investigation, not an actual recall order, and no formal recall action had been initiated.
ladder.L3:
Senator Mark Kelly, a retired Navy Captain, joined five other Democratic lawmakers in mid-November 2025 in releasing a video telling US troops they could refuse 'illegal orders.' President Trump responded by accusing the lawmakers of 'sedition punishable by DEATH,' and on November 24, 2025 the Pentagon publicly announced an investigation into Kelly, pointing to 10 U.S.C. provisions that allow the Secretary of Defense to recall retired members to active duty for purposes including court-martial. The Pentagon's statement was widely characterized in the press as extraordinary and politically charged, and many legal commentators and former JAG officers publicly questioned whether such a recall of a sitting senator would be lawful or practically feasible.

Several factors bear on the trajectory between the announcement and April 1, 2026: military investigations of this kind typically take many months to develop before any administrative or judicial action; a recall to active duty of a sitting member of Congress would be unprecedented and would likely trigger immediate litigation and constitutional challenges under the Speech or Debate Clause and separation-of-powers doctrine; and as of the Pentagon's November 24 statement, only an investigation — not a recall order — had been announced. Kelly himself publicly stated he would not be intimidated and continued his Senate duties, and no subsequent public reporting in the days following indicated that the Department of Defense had issued recall paperwork or moved beyond the investigative stage.

title: Will the United States impose additional sanctions on Russia related to the Ukraine war before March 14, 2026?
background:
The United States has repeatedly imposed a variety of sanctions on Russia in recent years. In April 2013, under the Barack Obama administration, the United States imposed sanctions on numerous Russian officials under the [Magnitsky Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnitsky_Act), which had been signed into law the previous year. Then, in March 2014, the United States and the European Union [imposed sanctions on numerous Russian officials](https://www.nytimes.com/2014/03/18/world/europe/us-imposes-new-sanctions-on-russian-officials.html?hp&_r=0) in connection with the Russian occupation of Crimea. (The US ultimately imposed [multiple rounds of sanctions](https://www.state.gov/division-for-counter-threat-finance-and-sanctions/ukraine-and-russia-sanctions) related to that conflict.) And in December 2016, President Obama imposed [additional sanctions](https://www.wsj.com/articles/u-s-punishes-russia-over-election-hacking-with-sanctions-1483039178) on Russia in connection with the country's alleged interference in the 2016 US elections.

In 2017, Donald Trump came to power, taking a notably more conciliatory approach toward Russia than his predecessor had. Nevertheless, in July 2017, Congress passed the [Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countering_America%27s_Adversaries_Through_Sanctions_Act), which imposed new sanctions on Russia for its activities relating to Ukraine, Syria, and the 2016 election. Though he criticized the legislation as flawed, President Trump signed it into law. The Trump administration subsequently imposed [numerous other sanctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_sanctions_during_the_Russo-Ukrainian_war#2018) relating to Russia.

In February 2022, Russia invaded Ukraine, triggering ["the most severe economic sanctions ever levied on Russia."](https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/russia-economic-sanctions-ukraine-60-minutes-2022-03-20/) And as that conflict drags on, sanctions remain a key component of US foreign policy vis-à-vis Russia. On December 17, 2025, [Reuters reported](https://www.reuters.com/world/us-readies-new-russia-sanctions-if-putin-rejects-peace-deal-bloomberg-news-2025-12-17/) that the Trump administration was preparing an additional round of sanctions on Russia to pressure it to negotiate a peace with Ukraine.
resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as **Yes** if, after January 12, 2026 and before March 14, 2026 ET, the US government announces via binding legal action a new or expanded sanctions-related restriction on Russian persons or entities and the official announcement explicitly states it is related to the Ukraine war.

Sanctions include, but are not limited to asset freezes, transaction bans, trade restrictions, Entity List-type actions, or visa/entry restrictions, and they might be issued by OFAC, the Department of State, the Department of Commerce, the White House, or Congress.

Actions not explicitly linked to the war in the official announcements or press materials do not count, even if plausibly war-motivated.

ladder.L1: The United States has imposed numerous rounds of sanctions on Russia since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, using authorities at OFAC, the State Department, and the Department of Commerce. Sanctions policy toward Russia has been a recurring instrument across both the Biden and second Trump administrations.
ladder.L2: On December 17, 2025, Reuters reported that the Trump administration was preparing new sanctions on Russia to pressure Moscow into a peace deal, but the action was framed as contingent on Putin rejecting negotiations. Throughout late 2025, the Trump administration's public posture emphasized diplomacy and a negotiated settlement rather than escalating economic pressure, and several previously threatened sanctions packages had been delayed or held in reserve as leverage.
ladder.L3:
By late 2025, US sanctions policy toward Russia was being used primarily as conditional leverage in ongoing peace negotiations rather than as a steady stream of new designations. A December 17, 2025 Reuters report (citing Bloomberg) indicated the Trump administration had prepared an additional sanctions package but was holding it back contingent on whether Putin rejected a proposed peace framework. President Trump had publicly expressed reluctance to impose further economic measures while talks were active, and his administration had previously allowed some sanctions deadlines and threats to lapse without follow-through. Congressional efforts, including a bipartisan Russia sanctions bill led by Senator Lindsey Graham, had stalled through 2025 as the White House asked lawmakers to defer action to preserve diplomatic flexibility.

Additionally, the question's resolution criteria require not only a new binding sanctions action between January 12 and March 14, 2026, but also that the official announcement explicitly tie the measure to the Ukraine war. Historically, a meaningful share of Russia-related US designations in 2025 were framed under other authorities (e.g., cyber, narcotics, sanctions evasion, or Iran/North Korea-related secondary sanctions) without explicit Ukraine-war language, which narrows the set of actions that would qualify under the strict resolution criteria.

title: Will any NVIDIA GPUs better than the H200 be allowed to be exported to China before March 14, 2026?
background:
In October 2022, the US Department of Commerce enacted [export controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_New_Export_Controls_on_Advanced_Computing_and_Semiconductors_to_China) to limit the People's Republic of China's access to advanced computing chips and semiconductors, citing national security and foreign policy concerns. Initially, these rules were not aimed at restricting China's capacity to train large language models. However, they directly restricted the class of high-end GPUs that subsequently became central to generative AI, leading to an eventual shift in the controls' focus to encompass such issues.

In response to these restrictions, NVIDIA repeatedly designed China-specific variants of its chips that complied with the export controls. These initially included the A800 and H800 chips, which were later banned [after an update to the export regulations](https://www.reuters.com/technology/nvidia-may-be-forced-shift-out-some-countries-after-new-us-export-curbs-2023-10-17/), and then the H20, which was [only briefly restricted in early 2025](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/us-licenses-nvidia-export-chips-china-official-says-2025-08-08/). In late 2025, [reporting indicated](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/us-block-nvidias-sale-scaled-back-ai-chips-china-information-says-2025-11-07/) the US planned to block a new, highly capable China-specific chip referred to as B30A. Subsequently, however, President Trump announced, in a policy shift, that the US would permit [exports of the powerful H200 chip to China](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/nvidia-aims-begin-h200-chip-shipments-china-by-mid-february-sources-say-2025-12-22/), subject to a 25% fee.
resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as **Yes** if, after January 12, 2026 and before March 14, 2026 ET, the US government publicly states that it will permit any Nvidia GPU that is better than the H200 to be exported to mainland China.

This question will also resolve as **Yes** if such GPUs are directly exported to mainland China, without [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions) reporting that the export violated US export controls or that the US government is taking enforcement action relating to those exports, before March 14, 2026 ET.

For the purposes of this question, "better than H200" is defined as any GPU with both:

* a peak FP8 Tensor Core throughput (including sparsity) higher than 4 petaFLOPS

and

* an HBM bandwidth of at least 4.8 TB/s.

ladder.L1: The US has maintained export controls on advanced AI chips to China since October 2022, with periodic updates. NVIDIA has responded by designing China-specific variants of its GPUs to comply with evolving rules, and policy on which chips may be sold to China has shifted several times.
ladder.L2: As of late December 2025, the most powerful NVIDIA chip publicly cleared for export to China was the H200, following a Trump administration policy shift that allowed H200 sales subject to a 25% fee. Reporting in November 2025 indicated the US planned to block the more capable B30A China-specific chip. No public US government statement has authorized export of GPUs more capable than the H200 to mainland China, and NVIDIA's H200 shipments to China were reported to be targeted to begin only by mid-February 2026.
ladder.L3:
The trajectory of US export controls through late 2025 shows incremental, contested loosening rather than broad authorization of frontier chips for China. After tightening controls in 2023 that banned the A800 and H800, the US briefly restricted and then re-permitted the H20 in 2025. In November 2025, Reuters reported the administration intended to block NVIDIA's new China-specific B30A chip, which would have been more capable than chips previously allowed. In December 2025, President Trump announced a policy shift permitting H200 exports to China subject to a 25% fee, with NVIDIA reportedly aiming to begin H200 shipments by mid-February 2026.

Taken together, the public record through the question's start window establishes the H200 as the explicit ceiling of permitted exports, with the next-tier chip (B30A) reportedly blocked and no announced pathway for chips exceeding the H200's FP8 throughput and HBM bandwidth thresholds. US chip-export policy changes have historically required formal Commerce Department action or explicit presidential announcement, and the logistics of even the newly-permitted H200 shipments were still being arranged as the resolution window opened.

title: Will the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Louisiana v. Callais hold that race-conscious districting is unconstitutional?
resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as Yes if the U.S. Supreme Court's final merits decision in [*Louisiana v. Callais*](https://www.supremecourt.gov/search.aspx?filename=/docket/docketfiles/html/public/24-109.html) holds that race-conscious districting, even when done to comply with Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, is unconstitutional.

This question will resolve as No if the Supreme Court's decision upholds the challenged Louisiana map or otherwise resolves the case without holding that race-conscious districting is impermissible.

If the Supreme Court does not issue a merits decision in *Louisiana v. Callais* before January 1, 2027, this question will be annulled.

ladder.L1: Louisiana v. Callais is a case before the U.S. Supreme Court concerning a Louisiana congressional districting map that was drawn following litigation under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. The case raises questions about the interaction between the Voting Rights Act's requirements and the Equal Protection Clause's limits on the use of race in redistricting.
ladder.L2: The Louisiana map at issue in Callais was drawn after a federal court found the state's prior map likely violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, and the Supreme Court in Allen v. Milligan (2023) reaffirmed Section 2's application to redistricting and rejected arguments that it requires a race-neutral approach. After oral argument in the 2024-2025 term, the Supreme Court took the unusual step of ordering reargument and requesting supplemental briefing, rather than issuing a decision, signaling the Court was not prepared to issue a sweeping ruling at that time.
ladder.L3:
Louisiana v. Callais involves a challenge to Louisiana's congressional map that was drawn to include a second majority-Black district after a federal court found the prior map likely violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. The case sits against a recent precedent backdrop in which the Supreme Court, in Allen v. Milligan (2023), reaffirmed Section 2's application to redistricting by a 5-4 vote, with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh joining the Court's three liberals; Justice Kavanaugh wrote separately to note that race-based remedies under Section 2 may not extend indefinitely, but did not vote to strike them down. The Court has historically been cautious about issuing sweeping rulings that would invalidate a major federal civil rights statute, as seen in Shelby County (2013), which narrowly targeted the coverage formula rather than Section 5 itself.

After initial oral argument, the Court did not decide the case on its first hearing and instead set it for reargument with supplemental briefing on additional questions, a procedural move that often indicates internal division or a desire for narrower grounds of decision. Commentary from court observers and briefing from the parties suggested multiple possible off-ramps available to the Court, including resolving the case on record-specific or remedial grounds rather than reaching the broader constitutional question about whether race-conscious districting to comply with Section 2 is per se impermissible. Taken together, these facts indicate substantial institutional and doctrinal friction against a sweeping holding that race-conscious districting is unconstitutional.

title: Will the United States intervene militarily in Venezuela again before May 2026?
background:
On January 3, 2026, the United States launched a [surprise attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_strikes_in_Venezuela) on Venezuela, bombing military bases and infrastructure and capturing and removing President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from the country. This attack was the apparent culmination of a [months-long buildup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_military_buildup_in_the_Caribbean_during_Operation_Southern_Spear) of U.S. naval forces in the Caribbean Sea which included multiple airstrikes on boats off the coast of Venezuela, allegedly piloted by drug traffickers.

In the aftermath of the attack, there has been some confusion about the U.S. government's future intentions with respect to Venezuela. U.S. President Donald Trump has stated that [the U.S. was going to "run" Venezuela](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jan/03/trump-venezuela-oil-industry) but also indicated that Venezuela's Vice President, Delcy Rodríguez, would assume the presidency. (Rodríguez, for her part, denounced the attack and declared that Maduro remained the lawful President.) U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has [denied](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/04/us/politics/rubio-military-quarantine-venezuela-oil.html) that the U.S. would be involved in governing or occupying Venezuela, indicating that the U.S. simply intended to continue to put financial pressure on Venezuela's oil industry. The January 3, 2026 U.S. strike on Venezuela was the apparent culmination of a months-long buildup of naval forces in the Caribbean under Operation Southern Spear, during which the U.S. had already conducted multiple airstrikes on boats allegedly piloted by drug traffickers. The strike itself was extensive — hitting military bases and infrastructure — and resulted in the capture and removal of President Maduro and his wife from the country, suggesting the U.S. achieved its primary tactical objectives in a single operation.

Following the attack, U.S. messaging emphasized de-escalation of direct military involvement: Secretary Rubio explicitly denied that the U.S. would occupy or govern Venezuela, framing future U.S. policy as continued financial and oil-sector pressure rather than further kinetic action. Trump indicated Vice President Delcy Rodríguez would assume the presidency and cooperate with Washington, though Rodríguez publicly denounced the attack and affirmed Maduro as the lawful president. Trump also stated the U.S. was 'ready to stage a second and much larger attack if we need to do so,' phrasing that conditions any further strike on a perceived need. Taken together, the public posture combines a completed, large-scale operation with stated reluctance toward further military action absent a triggering development.
